q: 15 g of KCl is dissolved in 135 g of water. What is the percentage by mass of KCl in the solution?
x: Mass of solution = 15 + 135 = 150 g, so % KCl = 15/150 × 100 = 10%. Dividing by the mass of water (135 g) instead of the mass of solution gives the tempting 11.1%.

q: A sample of hard water contains 40 ppm of Ca²⁺ by mass. Taking its density as 1.00 g cm⁻³, what is the molar concentration of Ca²⁺ in the water? (Ca = 40)
x: 40 ppm means 40 g in 10⁶ g, i.e. 0.040 g in 1000 g = 1 dm³ of water. 0.040 g ÷ 40 g mol⁻¹ = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³. Forgetting to divide by the molar mass gives 4.0 × 10⁻² (that is grams per dm³, not moles).

q: Aluminium sulphate, Al₂(SO₄)₃, is fully dissociated in a 0.10 mol dm⁻³ aqueous solution. What is the concentration of sulphate ions?
x: Al₂(SO₄)₃ → 2Al³⁺ + 3SO₄²⁻, so [SO₄²⁻] = 3 × 0.10 = 0.30 mol dm⁻³. 0.20 mol dm⁻³ is the Al³⁺ concentration and 0.50 mol dm⁻³ is the total of all ions.

q: An aqueous solution is 20% NaOH by mass. What is its molality? (NaOH = 40 g mol⁻¹)
x: 100 g of solution holds 20 g NaOH (0.50 mol) in 80 g = 0.080 kg of water. Molality = 0.50/0.080 = 6.25 mol kg⁻¹. Dividing by the 100 g of solution instead of the 80 g of water gives 5.00 mol kg⁻¹.

q: What mass of copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, is needed to make 500 cm³ of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ CuSO₄ solution? (Cu = 63.5, S = 32, O = 16, H = 1)
x: Moles needed = 0.10 × 0.500 = 0.050 mol. Molar mass of CuSO₄·5H₂O = 63.5 + 32 + 64 + 90 = 249.5 g mol⁻¹, so mass = 0.050 × 249.5 ≈ 12.5 g. Using anhydrous CuSO₄ (159.5 g mol⁻¹) gives 8.0 g; forgetting the 500 cm³ gives 25.0 g.

q: A solution labelled 0.25 mol kg⁻¹ (molal) in NaCl contains 0.25 mol of NaCl in each:
x: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent, here water. Moles per dm³ of solution is molarity, the most common mix-up.

q: Which pair of liquids shows a positive deviation from Raoult's law?
x: In ethanol–water the ethanol–water attractions are weaker than the hydrogen bonding in the pure liquids, so the vapour pressure is higher than predicted and a minimum-boiling azeotrope (about 95.6% ethanol) forms. Nitric acid–water and chloroform–acetone show negative deviation; hexane–heptane is nearly ideal.

q: When concentrated nitric acid is mixed with water, the mixture becomes hot and its volume is slightly less than the sum of the volumes mixed. Compared with the value predicted by Raoult's law, the vapour pressure of this mixture is:
o: Equal to the sum of the vapour pressures of the pure liquids
x: Heat given out and a fall in volume show that the attractions between unlike molecules are stronger than in the pure liquids. Fewer molecules escape, so the vapour pressure is lower: a negative deviation. Higher would be the case for weaker unlike attractions.

q: Equal masses of liquid X (molar mass 50 g mol⁻¹) and liquid Y (molar mass 100 g mol⁻¹) are mixed and form an ideal solution. At the temperature used, pure X has a vapour pressure of 60 kPa and pure Y 30 kPa. What is the vapour pressure of the solution?
x: Take 100 g of each: 2 mol X and 1 mol Y, so x(X) = 2/3 and x(Y) = 1/3. P = (2/3)(60) + (1/3)(30) = 40 + 10 = 50 kPa. Treating equal masses as equal moles gives 45 kPa; 40 kPa is the partial pressure of X alone.

q: According to Raoult's law, the partial vapour pressure of a volatile component in an ideal solution equals:
o: Its mass fraction in the liquid × the vapour pressure of the pure component
Its mole fraction in the liquid ÷ the vapour pressure of the pure component
Its mole fraction in the liquid × the vapour pressure of the pure component
The vapour pressure of the pure component, whatever the composition
x: Raoult's law: p = x × p°, where x is the mole fraction of that component in the liquid and p° its vapour pressure when pure. The law uses mole fraction, not mass fraction.

q: Benzene and toluene form a nearly ideal solution; at a given temperature pure benzene has the higher vapour pressure. Compared with the liquid mixture, the vapour in equilibrium with it is:
x: Mole fraction of benzene in the vapour = x(benzene) × p°(benzene)/P, and p°(benzene) is greater than the total pressure P, so the vapour is richer in the more volatile benzene. It is not pure benzene, because toluene also has a vapour pressure.

q: What mass of ethylene glycol, C₂H₆O₂ (molar mass 62 g mol⁻¹), must be dissolved in 500 g of water to lower its freezing point to −3.72 °C? (Kf of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
x: ΔTf = Kf × m, so m = 3.72/1.86 = 2.0 mol kg⁻¹. In 0.500 kg of water that is 1.0 mol, i.e. 62 g. Forgetting that only 500 g of water is used gives 124 g.

q: An aqueous solution of a non-electrolyte has an osmotic pressure of 2.46 atm at 27 °C. Taking its molality to be equal to its molarity, at what temperature does it freeze? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, Kf of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹)
x: π = CRT gives C = 2.46/(0.0821 × 300) ≈ 0.10 mol dm⁻³, so m ≈ 0.10 mol kg⁻¹. ΔTf = 1.86 × 0.10 = 0.186 K, so it freezes at −0.186 °C. Using 27 instead of 300 K gives C ≈ 1.11 and the tempting −2.06 °C.

q: Dissolving 10 g of a non-volatile non-electrolyte in 180 g of water lowers the vapour pressure of the water by 1.0% at a given temperature. Approximately what is the molar mass of the solute?
x: Relative lowering = mole fraction of solute ≈ n(solute)/n(water) = 0.010. n(water) = 180/18 = 10 mol, so n(solute) ≈ 0.10 mol and M ≈ 10/0.10 = 100 g mol⁻¹. Reading 1.0% as 0.10 instead of 0.010 gives 10 g mol⁻¹.

q: Which colligative property is most suitable for finding the molar mass of a protein or a polymer?
x: For a large molecule even a few grams give very few moles, so the other effects are too small to measure, while osmotic pressure is still measurable and is taken at room temperature, where proteins are not damaged.

q: Seawater and pure water are separated by a semipermeable membrane. A pressure greater than the osmotic pressure of seawater is applied on the seawater side. What happens?
o: Water passes from the pure water into the seawater
Salt ions pass through into the pure water
No water moves across the membrane
Water passes from the seawater into the pure water
x: Applying more than the osmotic pressure reverses osmosis: solvent is pushed from the solution into the pure solvent, which is how seawater is desalinated. Without the extra pressure, water would move the other way (ordinary osmosis).

q: Which of these is an emulsion (a liquid dispersed in a liquid)?
x: Milk is liquid fat dispersed in water, an emulsion. Smoke is solid in gas, fog is liquid in gas (an aerosol) and pumice is gas in solid.

q: Which change is a hydrolysis rather than a hydration?
x: In hydrolysis a water molecule is split: here the acetate ion takes H⁺ from water and leaves OH⁻. In hydration whole water molecules simply attach to ions or form a hydrate, as in the other three changes.

q: In aqueous solution the hydrated Li⁺ ion is larger than the hydrated K⁺ ion, although the bare Li⁺ ion is much smaller. The reason is that Li⁺:
o: Has a larger nuclear charge than K⁺
Is less strongly hydrated than K⁺
Forms covalent bonds with the hydrogen atoms of water
Has a higher charge density, so it attracts and holds more water molecules
x: The same +1 charge on a much smaller ion gives Li⁺ a high charge density, so it binds a larger shell of water molecules and its hydration enthalpy is more exothermic. Li has only 3 protons against 19 in K, so the nuclear-charge option is wrong.

q: The particles of a sol such as iron(III) hydroxide sol do not join together and coagulate in the pure sol mainly because:
o: They are too small ever to collide with one another
All the particles carry the same kind of electric charge and repel one another
They are present as separate dissolved ions
They are lighter than the water molecules around them
x: Each colloidal particle adsorbs ions of one kind and so carries the same charge as the others; the repulsion keeps them apart. Adding an electrolyte neutralises this charge and causes coagulation.

q: 2.44 g of hydrated barium chloride, BaCl₂·xH₂O, is heated to constant mass, leaving 2.08 g of anhydrous BaCl₂. What is x? (BaCl₂ = 208 g mol⁻¹, H₂O = 18 g mol⁻¹)
x: Water lost = 2.44 − 2.08 = 0.36 g = 0.020 mol; BaCl₂ = 2.08/208 = 0.010 mol. Ratio 0.020 : 0.010 = 2, so x = 2. Halving the moles of water by mistake (for example dividing 0.36 by 36) gives the tempting 1.
